subject: Climate & Environment
title: Retrofitting Old Buildings
description: A short lesson to help you apply Retrofitting Old Buildings.

hook.text: You can't demolish every old building. But you can make them dramatically more efficient.

buildup.text: Adding insulation, replacing windows, and installing heat pumps can cut energy use by 50 to 80%.

discovery.text: The Netherlands is retrofitting millions of homes to be gas-free by 2050 — a national program.

twist.text: Deep retrofits are expensive. Without government subsidies, most homeowners can't afford them.

climax.text: Every uninsulated building is leaking energy and money. The payoff is enormous at scale.

punchline.text: The greenest building is the one already standing — just made smarter.

quiz.question: How much can a deep retrofit reduce a building's energy use?

details.summary: Most buildings standing in 2050 have already been built, making energy retrofits essential for meeting climate targets. Retrofitting involves adding insulation, upgrading windows, replacing fossil heating with heat pumps, and improving controls, often cutting energy use by 50 to 75 percent.
details.whyItMatters: New construction alone cannot decarbonize the building sector fast enough. Retrofitting the existing stock is necessary to close the gap between current emissions and climate goals.
takeaways: Most 2050 buildings already exist and need efficiency upgrades
Deep retrofits can cut energy use by 50 to 75 percent
Heat pump installation is a key retrofit measure

faq.question: What does a deep energy retrofit involve?
faq.answer: A deep retrofit typically includes adding external or cavity insulation, replacing windows with double or triple glazing, installing a heat pump, upgrading ventilation with heat recovery, and adding smart controls. The goal is to reduce energy demand by at least 50 percent.

faq.question: Why is the retrofit rate so low?
faq.answer: Globally, less than 1 percent of existing buildings are deeply retrofitted each year. Barriers include high upfront costs, fragmented ownership in multi-unit buildings, disruption to occupants, and lack of skilled labor. Policy incentives are needed to accelerate the pace.
